title: Job 24:13–25
context: Job continues, now describing those who rebel against the light: the murderer, the adulterer, those who dig through houses in the dark and shut themselves up by day. From 24:18 the flow becomes hard to follow. The wicked are called foam on the waters, their portion cursed; drought and Sheol are said to consume those who have sinned; then God is said to preserve the mighty and to give them security, and then they are exalted only a little while and are cut off like the tops of the grain. Readers have understood this stretch in more than one way: as Job’s own account of a delayed but coming end, as a conventional picture he recites or contests, or as a description of present security mixed with a later fall. The notes do not choose a reconstruction, and they do not rearrange the verses. WEB’s order is the order to be read, with the difficulty named. Job ends with a challenge: if it is not so now, who will prove him a liar? The unit remains his protest, not a finished theodicy. Both traditions handle 24:18–24 with that hedge, and they invent no party contrast over a solution the text does not give.

verses.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job says, “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths.” The “these” points to people who will now be named by their deeds in the dark. Rebellion against the light is his heading for murderer, adulterer, and house-breaker in the verses that follow. The speaker is still Job.

Arminian readers take the rebellion against the light as Job’s moral description of such people, a protest, not a riddle about Israel’s law in particular.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a class of people who will not stay in the light’s paths, the heading of a short catalogue, still in Job’s voice, still not the narrator’s later verdict on the friends.

Both traditions keep the verse as Job’s introduction of the night-workers, and invent no contrast over the image of light.

verses.text: The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief.
verses.arminianNotes:
The murderer rises with the light, kills the poor and needy, and in the night is like a thief. The first example is that murderer. The verse should be told as Job tells it, with restraint, the poor again the victims, as in 24:2–12.

Arminian readers hear a real charge against those who kill the weak and steal in the night, Job still speaking of the murderer, not of himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the poor and needy as the ones killed, and the night as the murderer’s other hour, a continuation of the protest, not a confession.

Both traditions report the line soberly and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye will see me.’ He disguises his face.
verses.arminianNotes:
The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, “No eye will see me.” The adulterer disguises his face. Job is describing secret sin that counts on not being seen, a human claim of hiddenness, not a doctrine that God in fact does not see.

Arminian readers take the waiting and the disguise as Job’s picture of a man who hides from human eyes, the saying “No eye will see me” being the adulterer’s, not Job’s theology.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the twilight and the disguised face in the adulterer’s practice, a claim of invisibility Job is exposing, not granting as the truth about God’s sight.

Both traditions keep the quoted saying in the adulterer’s mouth and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light.” The catalogue continues with those who break into houses at night and hide by day, people who “don’t know the light.” The darkness is their chosen cover, matching 24:13.

Arminian readers take the digging and the daytime shutting-up as Job’s report of calculated crime, work done out of the light.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear houses broken in the dark and a refusal of the day, still Job’s description of such people, not a symbol requiring a second sense.

Both traditions leave the verse in the night-catalogue and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: For the morning is to all of them like thick darkness, for they know the terrors of the thick darkness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the morning is to all of them like thick darkness, for they know the terrors of the thick darkness.” Morning itself is, to them, like thick darkness; they know the terrors of that darkness. The line closes the night-section by saying that the light is no comfort to people who live by the dark.

Arminian readers hear a moral reversal, morning felt as darkness by those who have made the night their cover, Job still describing, not yet turning to the difficult lines that follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the morning as terror to them, the thick darkness as what they know, a close of 24:13–17 before the harder flow of 24:18–24.

Both traditions keep the verse with the rebels against the light, and invent no contrast over the image.

verses.text: “They are foam on the surface of the waters. Their portion is cursed on the earth. They don’t turn into the way of the vineyards.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job says, “They are foam on the surface of the waters. Their portion is cursed on the earth. They don’t turn into the way of the vineyards.” From here the subject and the tone are harder to fix. The wicked are likened to foam, their portion cursed, their path not the vineyards’ path. Some hear a sudden turn to the wicked’s instability or to a conventional curse; some hear Job reciting a view he does not simply grant. The notes do not decide among those readings, and they do not move the verse from its place.

Arminian readers take the foam and the cursed portion as the text stands, a difficult turn after the catalogue of unpunished harm, to be read with a hedge, not solved by a theory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the three sentences in WEB’s order, naming the difficulty of the flow, without asserting that the lines have been misplaced or that a lost speaker must be supplied.

Both traditions hedge the turn at 24:18 and invent no contrast over a reconstruction they refuse to make.

verses.text: Drought and heat consume the snow waters, so does Sheol those who have sinned.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Drought and heat consume the snow waters, so does Sheol those who have sinned.” As drought and heat take the snow waters, so Sheol, the place of the dead, takes those who have sinned. The comparison is of a sure consuming. How this sits with 24:1–12, where the wicked seem to flourish, is part of the same difficulty already named; the notes do not force a single resolution.

Arminian readers take the comparison as it is written, a word about Sheol consuming sinners, held beside the earlier protest, not used to cancel it or to rewrite it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep drought, heat, and Sheol in the verse’s own analogy, and they refuse to rearrange the line in order to make chapter 24 speak with one easy voice.

Both traditions report the saying, hedge its place in the argument, and invent no contrast over Sheol.

verses.text: The womb will forget him. The worm will feed sweetly on him. He will be no more remembered. Unrighteousness will be broken as a tree.
verses.arminianNotes:
The womb will forget him, and the worm will feed sweetly on him; the wicked will be no more remembered, and unrighteousness will be broken as a tree. The end of the wicked is pictured as forgetting, the worm, a name lost, and unrighteousness broken like a tree. The lines sound like a conventional fate of the evildoer. In this chapter they follow a long account of harm that has not yet been stopped. The tension is to be named, not erased by a theory of quotation or of a later editor.

Arminian readers hear a strong picture of an end, and they keep it in Job’s speech as WEB orders it, without claiming to have settled how it relates to 24:12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the womb, the worm, the forgotten name, and the broken tree stand, a hard sequence, not a problem to be solved by moving verses.

Both traditions hedge the flow and invent no contrast over the images.

verses.text: He devours the barren who don’t bear. He shows no kindness to the widow.
verses.arminianNotes:
The same stretch says that he devours the barren who don’t bear, and shows no kindness to the widow. The lines describe present cruelty, not yet the fall of 24:24. The grammar of the subject, after 24:20, is part of the difficult run, and the notes do not pretend to a certainty the verses withhold.

Arminian readers take the barren and the widow as victims still in view, a return to the tone of 24:3 and 24:9, heard with a hedge about the exact antecedent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a devouring and a lack of kindness to the widow, and they leave the subject as the text’s own pronoun, without supplying a name the verse does not give.

Both traditions stay close to the wording, hedge the connection, and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: Yet God preserves the mighty by his power. He rises up who has no assurance of life.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet God preserves the mighty by his power.” A man then rises up who has no assurance of life. The “Yet” is difficult. God is said to preserve the mighty by his power. Some hear God prolonging the powerful, in tension with 24:18–20; some hear a different turn. The notes report the sentences as WEB has them and do not assert a reconstruction that would make the “Yet” easy.

Arminian readers take the preserving of the mighty as a hard word in Job’s protest, possibly the security of oppressors, and they leave the exact force of “Yet” open.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep God as the one who preserves the mighty in this line, and the rising of the one without assurance of life, without rearranging the verse to fit a preferred argument.

Both traditions hedge the connector and invent no contrast over a solution they do not have.

verses.text: God gives them security, and they rest in it. His eyes are on their ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
“God gives them security, and they rest in it.” God’s eyes, Job adds, are on their ways. The second sentence may comfort or may trouble: eyes on their ways can mean attention that will judge, or attention that seems to let them rest. Job does not pause to explain. The security sits beside the short exaltation of 24:24, and the whole should be read with the same hedge already named for 24:18–24.

Arminian readers hear a real tension, security given and eyes upon their ways, and they refuse to decide more than the two sentences say.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the gift of security and the eyes on their ways as Job’s wording, not a system of providence worked out in advance, and not a denial that God sees.

Both traditions share that God’s eyes are not shut, and they invent no contrast over the rest the mighty are said to have.

verses.text: They are exalted; yet a little while, and they are gone. Yes, they are brought low, they are taken out of the way as all others, and are cut off as the tops of the ears of grain.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They are exalted; yet a little while, and they are gone. Yes, they are brought low, they are taken out of the way as all others, and are cut off as the tops of the ears of grain.” Exaltation lasts only a little while; then they are gone, brought low, taken out of the way, cut off like the tops of the grain. If 24:22–23 have described security, this verse describes its end. Job may be saying that the mighty do fall at last, even if their fall is delayed; he may be saying more, or less. The notes do not press a single scheme onto the comparison with grain.

Arminian readers take the little while and the cutting off as Job’s word that exaltation is not the last fact, a hope or an observation spoken after a long catalogue of delay, still not a finished theodicy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a short exaltation and a certain cutting off, in WEB’s order after the security of 24:23, without claiming to have resolved the whole run from 24:18 to this close.

Both traditions keep the grain image as a picture of being cut off, hedge the argument’s shape, and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: If it isn’t so now, who will prove me a liar, and make my speech worth nothing?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Job ends, “If it isn’t so now, who will prove me a liar, and make my speech worth nothing?” Job puts his speech on the table and dares a refutation: if it is not so now, who will prove him a liar? The “now” matters. Job is appealing to how things stand, the visible delay and the visible wrong, not withdrawing the protest. The challenge closes chapters 23–24 as Job’s word, still awaiting the rest of the book, not as a theodicy already won.

Arminian readers take the challenge as a real invitation to be answered, Job standing by his speech, open to being proved wrong, not claiming a last and unanswerable system.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear Job binding himself to what he has said, a demand for a reply, not a claim that the argument of chapter 24 has been made simple.

Both traditions leave the dare as the close of the unit, and they invent no contrast over a speech Job himself has submitted to be tested.
